object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event representing something that broke; tracked from triage through closure.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A monitoring-platform-generated signal (automatic or manual) that can be an origin for an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? ... Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, issued by the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised by or on behalf of a customer, which can be an origin for an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a support ticket, in the ticketing system's own format.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact/blast-radius classification of an incident, SEV1 (worst) to SEV4 (least).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer-urgency classification of an incident, P1 (worst) to P4 (least), independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Commander
object_types.definition: The named person acting as incident commander for the duration of a declared incident; a role, not a job title.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by incidents, owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Commander is described as identified by name only ('One person, named'); no formal reference scheme (like an employee ID) is given, and 'Commander' as a person may overlap with other person-related concepts (e.g., service owner is a team, not a person). Is Commander identified by name alone, or should it link to an Employee/Person entity with its own ID?

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged by stakeholders as overloaded, referring both to the Commander (incident-specific role) and the Service Owner (standing team assignment). This is captured as two distinct fact types, but the transcript notes ongoing real-world ambiguity in channel communication -- worth flagging for downstream consumers/UI design.

source_references.excerpt: the second collision. The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing... And in a channel, 'who owns this?' means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised...'), with only current value modeled on the Incident and history captured 'in the timeline, as events' -- an unmodeled concept. Should a Timeline/Event entity be added to capture historical severity/priority/state changes, or is current-state-only sufficient for this model?

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius... Is the history of that kept? ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between Priority and Severity is explicitly stated to be independent (not derivable one from the other), but no correlation table or joint constraint is given -- confirmed as fully independent value assignments with no cross-constraint needed.

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all? ... The point stands either way -- they're independent.

ambiguities.description: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and parked pending a decision from Ravi. No 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... Parking it explicitly, then. ... The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status mentioned by Owen is explicitly excluded from the model since it is not a formal system state, but this suggests informal/undocumented sub-states may exist in practice that could later need capturing.

source_references.excerpt: There's also 'monitoring,' which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... That's not a state ... It's not in the dropdown. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate-of ring constraint is intended to be acyclic and to disallow chains (each duplicate should point directly at the ultimate primary), but this is explicitly stated as 'not enforced' in the actual system. Should the model enforce this as a hard constraint, or reflect the current unenforced reality (potential chains) for accuracy?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? ... nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... It's wrong... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Incident-Service 'affects' relationship cardinality on the Service side is not fully specified (can a single service be affected by many incidents concurrently, historically, or both) -- likely yes, but not explicitly confirmed with an example.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? ... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.
